q: Magnetism is a phenomenon associated with _____.
e: Magnetism is a phenomenon associated with magnetic field. Magnetic field here means the region around a magnet where magnetic effects show up. Electric field: the influence around electric charge, not the field of a magnet.

q: A magnet has a _____ around it.
e: A magnet has a magnetic field around it. Magnetic field here means the region around a magnet where magnetic effects show up. Electric current: the flow of electric charge.

q: Magnets are materials which exhibit magnetic properties such as attracting magnetic materials, having two poles, and _____.
a: like poles attract, unlike poles repel
like poles repel, unlike poles attract
e: Magnets are materials which exhibit magnetic properties such as attracting magnetic materials, having two poles, and like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract here means the two ends of a magnet, north and south. Like poles attract, unlike poles repel: the two ends of a magnet, north and south.

q: Magnetite consists of an oxide of _____.
e: Magnetite consists of an oxide of iron. Iron here means the metal in magnetite and the common magnetic element.

q: Materials such as cobalt, nickel, and some alloys such as steel are called _____.
e: Materials such as cobalt, nickel, and some alloys such as steel are called magnetic materials. Magnetic materials here means materials a magnet can attract, such as iron, cobalt, nickel, and steel. Non-magnetic materials: materials a magnet does not attract, such as brass, copper, wood, and plastic.

q: Materials such as brass, copper, wood, and plastics that are not attracted by a magnet are called _____.
e: Materials such as brass, copper, wood, and plastics that are not attracted by a magnet are called non-magnetic materials. Non-magnetic materials here means materials a magnet does not attract, such as brass, copper, wood, and plastic.

q: Any material that is able to keep its magnetism for a long time is called a _____.
e: Any material that is able to keep its magnetism for a long time is called a permanent magnet. Permanent magnet here means a body that attracts iron and has two poles. Temporary magnet: a body that attracts iron and has two poles.

q: Modern-day permanent magnets are usually made of steel and special alloys such as alcomax and _____.
e: Modern-day permanent magnets are usually made of steel and special alloys such as alcomax and alnico. Alnico here means an alloy used for strong permanent magnets, with aluminium, nickel, and cobalt.

q: Alcomax and alnico contain metals such as iron, nickel, copper, cobalt, and _____.
e: Alcomax and alnico contain metals such as iron, nickel, copper, cobalt, and aluminium. The physics in this sentence is built around aluminium.

q: Ceramic magnet is made from powders called _____.
e: Ceramic magnet is made from powders called ferrites. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Ferrites are compounds of iron oxide with _____.
e: Ferrites are compounds of iron oxide with other metal oxides. The physics in this sentence is built around other metal oxides.

q: Ceramic magnets are known to be _____.
e: Ceramic magnets are known to be brittle. Brittle here means easy to snap, the opposite of flexible.

q: The two ends of the magnet where most steel pins are attracted are called the _____ of the magnet.
e: The two ends of the magnet where most steel pins are attracted are called the poles of the magnet. Poles here means the two ends of a magnet, north and south.

q: When a suspended bar magnet comes to rest, one end always points towards the northern end of the Earth. This end is called the _____.
e: When a suspended bar magnet comes to rest, one end always points towards the northern end of the Earth. This end is called the north-seeking pole. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The north-seeking pole and south-seeking pole of the magnet are usually referred to as simply the north pole ($N$-pole) and the _____.
e: The north-seeking pole and south-seeking pole of the magnet are usually referred to as simply the north pole ($N$-pole) and the south pole ($S$-pole). Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: According to the law of magnetic poles, like poles _____ and unlike poles attract.
e: According to the law of magnetic poles, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The physics in this sentence is built around repel.

q: A magnet can be used as a _____ for navigation.
e: A magnet can be used as a compass for navigation. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart involving navigation.

q: Magnetic pole strength is a measure of the _____ of magnetic poles.
e: Magnetic pole strength is a measure of the strength of magnetic poles. The physics in this sentence is built around strength.

q: The force between two poles is directly proportional to the product of the pole strengths and _____ proportional to the distance squared between them.
e: The force between two poles is directly proportional to the product of the pole strengths and inversely proportional to the distance squared between them. The physics in this sentence is built around inversely.

q: When a magnetised steel bar is cut into smaller pieces, every piece is a magnet with a(n) _____ and $S$-pole.
e: When a magnetised steel bar is cut into smaller pieces, every piece is a magnet with a(n) $N$-pole and $S$-pole. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: A magnetised bar is composed of tiny magnets all lined up with their $N$-poles pointing in the _____.
e: A magnetised bar is composed of tiny magnets all lined up with their $N$-poles pointing in the same direction. Same direction here means lined up together, which is how a bar becomes magnetised. Random direction: pointing every which way, so the tiny magnets cancel.

q: In an unmagnetised bar, the 'tiny' magnets point in a _____ direction.
e: In an unmagnetised bar, the 'tiny' magnets point in a random direction. Random here means pointing every which way, so the tiny magnets cancel.

q: In an unmagnetised bar, the resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is _____ out.
e: In an unmagnetised bar, the resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is cancelled out. Cancelled here means the tiny magnets point randomly, so the bar has no net pole.

q: The magnetic field is a region where _____ can be detected.
e: The magnetic field is a region where magnetic effects can be detected. A magnetic field line leaves the north pole and returns into the south pole involving where.

q: Distribution of magnetic field can be visualized by the _____.
e: Distribution of magnetic field can be visualized by the magnetic lines of force. Magnetic lines of force here means a push or pull that can change a body's state of motion. Electric lines of force: a push or pull that can change a body's state of motion.

q: The magnetic lines of force leave the _____ pole and enter the south pole.
e: The magnetic lines of force leave the north pole and enter the south pole. The physics in this sentence is built around north.

q: To show the pattern of a magnetic field around a bar magnet, we can sprinkle _____ lightly on a paper.
e: To show the pattern of a magnetic field around a bar magnet, we can sprinkle iron filings lightly on a paper. Iron filings here means the metal in magnetite and the common magnetic element.

q: The Earth has a _____.
e: The Earth has a magnetic field. Magnetic field here means the region around a magnet where magnetic effects show up.

q: We can think of the Earth as having an imaginary bar magnet inside it with magnetic north and _____ poles.
e: We can think of the Earth as having an imaginary bar magnet inside it with magnetic north and south poles. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The magnetic north lies somewhere in the sea in northern _____ but has been shifting slowly over the years.
e: The magnetic north lies somewhere in the sea in northern Canada but has been shifting slowly over the years. The physics in this sentence is built around Canada involving somewhere.

q: A magnetic field has neither a starting point nor an end point because magnets never have a _____.
e: A magnetic field has neither a starting point nor an end point because magnets never have a monopole. A magnetic field line leaves the north pole and returns into the south pole.

q: A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called _____.
e: A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called magnetisation. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart involving material.

q: Two types of magnetisation are magnetisation by stroking and magnetisation using _____.
e: Two types of magnetisation are magnetisation by stroking and magnetisation using direct current. Direct current here means the flow of electric charge. Alternating current: the flow of electric charge.

q: The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an _____.
e: The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an electric current. Electric current here means the flow of electric charge. Electric field: the influence around electric charge, not the field of a magnet.

q: A steel bar placed inside a solenoid with direct current passed through it becomes a _____.
e: A steel bar placed inside a solenoid with direct current passed through it becomes a permanent magnet. Permanent magnet here means a body that attracts iron and has two poles. Temporary magnet: a body that attracts iron and has two poles.

q: If an iron bar is placed inside a solenoid with direct current, it becomes magnetised temporarily as a(n) _____.
e: If an iron bar is placed inside a solenoid with direct current, it becomes magnetised temporarily as a(n) electromagnet. The physics in this sentence is built around electromagnet. Permanent magnet: a body that attracts iron and has two poles.

q: The polarities of the magnet produced by a solenoid depend on the _____ of the electric current.
e: The polarities of the magnet produced by a solenoid depend on the direction of the electric current. Current is charge passing a point per second.

q: In magnetisation by stroking, the magnet must be lifted _____ above the bar between successive strokes.
e: In magnetisation by stroking, the magnet must be lifted high above the bar between successive strokes. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the _____ polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it.
e: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the opposite polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart. Same: lined up together, which is how a bar becomes magnetised.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is attracted and becomes a magnet itself. This is called _____.
e: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is attracted and becomes a magnet itself. This is called induced magnetism. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In induced magnetism, the north pole of the permanent magnet induces a(n) _____ in the near end of the soft iron.
e: In induced magnetism, the north pole of the permanent magnet induces a(n) $S$-pole in the near end of the soft iron. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In induced magnetism, the far end of the soft iron becomes a(n) _____.
e: In induced magnetism, the far end of the soft iron becomes a(n) $N$-pole. The physics in this sentence is built around $N$-pole.

q: Iron is an element while steel is an alloy comprised of iron and _____.
e: Iron is an element while steel is an alloy comprised of iron and carbon. The physics in this sentence is built around carbon involving steel.

q: Magnetic materials such as steel which are harder to magnetise but retain their magnetism longer are called _____ magnetic materials.
e: Magnetic materials such as steel which are harder to magnetise but retain their magnetism longer are called hard magnetic materials. Hard names magnetic materials such as steel which are harder to magnetise but retain their magnetism longer.

q: Magnetic materials such as iron or special alloys like mumetal alloy which are easier to magnetise but do not retain their magnetism very long are called _____ magnetic materials.
e: Magnetic materials such as iron or special alloys like mumetal alloy which are easier to magnetise but do not retain their magnetism very long are called soft magnetic materials. The physics in this sentence is built around soft.

q: Soft iron can be _____ magnetised and demagnetised.
e: Soft iron can be easily magnetised and demagnetised. The physics in this sentence is built around easily.

q: Steel is hard to magnetise and _____ than iron.
e: Steel is hard to magnetise and demagnetise than iron. The physics in this sentence is built around demagnetise.

q: Soft iron can be magnetised by a _____ magnetic field.
e: Soft iron can be magnetised by a weak magnetic field. A magnetic field line leaves the north pole and returns into the south pole.

q: Steel requires a _____ magnetic field to magnetise.
e: Steel requires a strong magnetic field to magnetise. A magnetic field line leaves the north pole and returns into the south pole involving field involving magnetise.

q: Soft iron retains its magnetism _____.
e: Soft iron retains its magnetism temporarily. The physics in this sentence is built around temporarily.

q: Steel retains its magnetism _____.
e: Steel retains its magnetism permanently. The physics in this sentence is built around permanently involving magnetism.

q: Soft magnetic materials are used for transformers, electromagnets, magnetic shielding, electric bell, and _____.
e: Soft magnetic materials are used for transformers, electromagnets, magnetic shielding, electric bell, and magnetic relays. The physics in this sentence is built around magnetic relays.

q: Magnetic shielding is used to store magnetically sensitive instruments such as _____.
e: Magnetic shielding is used to store magnetically sensitive instruments such as watches. The physics in this sentence is built around watches involving store.
